scenes:
  - id: sc_1
    act_id: act_1
    header: EXT. RIVERSIDE BUS STOP - DUSK
    loc:
      type: EXT
      name: RIVERSIDE BUS STOP
      tod: DUSK
    shot_refs: []
    narrative: |-
      Rain drums on the roof of ADA's evacuation bus. Beyond the windscreen, the bridge disappears under brown water. Six neighbours wait inside. One carries a sleeping dog.

      IVO wheels a handcart down the bank. An old ferry bell hangs from its handle.

      @ADA
      The road behind us is gone.

      @IVO
      The ferry landing is higher.

      Ada looks at the narrow lane, then the water climbing the bus tyres.

      @ADA
      Can your boat carry us?

      Ivo doesn't answer. He takes the bell off the cart and rings it. Across the river, a warehouse light comes on.
    notes: Establish the goal and a limit the audience can see. Worked example. Adapt freely or use the companion outline to start your own story.
    extensions:
      x-skeleton:

          version: 1
          format: fountain
          speakers:
            ADA: char_1
            IVO: char_2
  - id: sc_2
    act_id: act_1
    header: EXT. OLD FERRY LANDING - DUSK
    loc:
      type: EXT
      name: OLD FERRY LANDING
      tod: DUSK
    shot_refs: []
    narrative: |-
      The ferry sits crooked against the landing. Its deck is split. Across the water, a rescue launch noses out of the warehouse dock.

      @IVO
      I kept meaning to mend her.

      Ada parks on the rising lane. She opens the bus doors. The neighbours climb to a stone waiting shelter while Ivo watches his boat drag against its rope.

      The launch turns away from the landing. A fallen tree blocks its approach. Its searchlight sweeps past them.

      @ADA
      They can't see the steps.

      Ivo points upstream, where a white marker stands on a higher ledge.

      @IVO
      They can reach there. We used it before the road.

      He leaves the ferry bell in Ada's hand and leads the neighbours uphill.
    notes: Make the obstacle change the plan; let both characters contribute. Worked example. Adapt freely or use the companion outline to start your own story.
    extensions:
      x-skeleton:
        writing:
          version: 1
          format: fountain
          speakers:
            ADA: char_1
            IVO: char_2
  - id: sc_3
    act_id: act_1
    header: EXT. UPSTREAM LEDGE - NIGHT
    loc:
      type: EXT
      name: UPSTREAM LEDGE
      tod: NIGHT
    shot_refs: []
    narrative: |-
      At the ledge, Ada counts five neighbours. Ivo appears below them, helping the sixth around a fallen branch. The launch is already passing.

      Ada rings the ferry bell. The engine slows. A searchlight finds the white marker.

      The crew brings the launch alongside and helps everyone aboard. Ivo is last. He looks downstream. His ferry has broken loose, turning slowly into the dark.

      @ADA
      I'm sorry.

      @IVO
      It was a boat.

      He looks along the bench: six neighbours, one driver, one wet dog.

      @IVO
      This is the crossing.

      Ada puts the bell beside him. As the launch reaches the far bank, he lets her ring it.
    notes: Resolve the danger through established information and a changed choice. Worked example. Adapt freely or use the companion outline to start your own story.

acts:
  - id: act_1
    title: A Knock for Nobody
    scene_refs:
      - sc_1

scenes:
  - id: sc_1
    act_id: act_1
    header: INT. CARETAKER'S KITCHEN - NIGHT
    loc:
      type: INT
      name: CARETAKER'S KITCHEN
      tod: NIGHT
    shot_refs: []
    narrative: |-
      Leena counted the keys twice. Front door, back door, cellar. Three keys for an empty house. Mrs Vale's niece had left tea, clean sheets, and an envelope marked FOR THE FIRST NIGHT.

      Inside was a list in a careful hand. Turn off the kitchen tap. Leave the landing light on. If someone knocks, count the people in the house before you answer.

      Leena checked the tap. It was dry. She turned on the landing light, because old staircases deserved light whatever their owners believed. Then she wrote ONE in the margin beside the last instruction.

      At eleven, someone knocked at the front door.

      "Sorry," called a woman outside. "I've forgotten my keys."

      It was Leena's voice, right down to the little catch on sorry.
    notes: Plant a rule and a sensory detail before the threat becomes explicit. Worked example. Adapt freely or use the companion outline to start your own story.
    extensions:
      x-skeleton:
        writing:
          version: 1
          format: prose
  - id: sc_2
    act_id: act_1
    header: INT. FRONT HALL - NIGHT
    loc:
      type: INT
      name: FRONT HALL
      tod: NIGHT
    shot_refs: []
    narrative: |-
      Through the frosted glass Leena saw a woman in her yellow raincoat. Her own coat hung from the hook beside her. She touched its sleeve. Water ran down her wrist.

      "Open up," the woman said. "It's cold."

      Leena called the niece. The phone rang on the other side of the door.

      She backed into the kitchen. The note had another line beneath her pencilled ONE: And if you are alone, keep it that way. She couldn't remember whether it had been there before.

      The knocking moved to the back door.

      Then the cellar door.

      Then the inside of the cupboard above the kettle.

      Leena sat at the table, put all three keys under her palm, and said, "One."

      The cupboard became still.
    notes: Escalate through a changed detail rather than explaining the creature. Worked example. Adapt freely or use the companion outline to start your own story.
    extensions:
      x-skeleton:
        writing:
          version: 1
          format: prose
  - id: sc_3
    act_id: act_1
    header: INT. CARETAKER'S KITCHEN - DAWN
    loc:
      type: INT
      name: CARETAKER'S KITCHEN
      tod: DAWN
    shot_refs: []
    narrative: |-
      For the rest of the night, the voice tried other rooms. It wept once, quietly, with Leena's own exhausted breath. Each time she wanted to answer, she pressed her hand against the keys and counted herself.

      At dawn, birds began in the hedge. The landing light went out.

      Leena opened the front door. The step was empty and dry. Her raincoat on the hook was dry too.

      She left the keys at the niece's office and returned her fee. When asked whether anything was wrong with the house, she said yes, and gave the woman the note. She waited while it was read. She made her promise not to send anyone there alone.

      Only at home did Leena empty her pockets.

      Inside the envelope, beneath the folded instructions, lay a fourth key. Its paper tag read: LEENA'S FRONT DOOR.

      She put it in a glass jar, screwed the lid tight, and called her sister. This time, a voice she knew answered somewhere far away.
    notes: Pay off the established rule; leave one concrete trace of the encounter. Worked example. Adapt freely or use the companion outline to start your own story.
    extensions:
      x-skeleton:
        writing:
          version: 1
          format: prose

    name: Leena
    notes: A practical caretaker beginning her first night in an empty house.
  - id: char_2
    name: Mrs Vale
    notes: The late owner, present through the instructions she left behind.

    title: The Uncollected Coat

scenes:
  - id: sc_1
    act_id: act_1
    header: INT. REPAIR SHOP - MORNING
    loc:
      type: INT
      name: REPAIR SHOP
      tod: MORNING
    shot_refs: []
    narrative: |-
      MINA unpicks a sleeve at the counter. Around her, empty hangers scrape as RAFI takes them down.

      @RAFI
      The landlord comes at four.

      @MINA
      Then we have six hours.

      @RAFI
      You said that yesterday.

      A green coat hangs alone beneath a card: ELISE — THURSDAY. No price.

      Rafi reaches for it. Mina catches the hanger.

      @MINA
      Someone is coming for that.

      @RAFI
      Mum wrote Thursday on everything she couldn't finish.

      Mina lays the coat across the counter as if someone has sat down between them.
    notes: Let a practical disagreement carry the emotional conflict. Worked example. Adapt freely or use the companion outline to start your own story.
    extensions:
      x-skeleton:
        writing:
          version: 1
          format: fountain
          speakers:
            RAFI: char_1
            MINA: char_2
            ELISE: char_3
  - id: sc_2
    act_id: act_1
    header: INT. REPAIR SHOP - AFTERNOON
    loc:
      type: INT
      name: REPAIR SHOP
      tod: AFTERNOON
    shot_refs: []
    narrative: |-
      ELISE arrives carrying a jar of buttons. She sees the bare rails and stops.

      @ELISE
      I only heard this morning.

      Mina nods. Rafi brings out the green coat.

      @RAFI
      There's nothing owing.

      @ELISE
      I know. I paid in March.

      She touches the sleeve. Inside its lining, uneven stitches form a small rectangle.

      @ELISE
      My hands shake. Your mother was teaching me. Every Thursday, a little more.

      Mina looks at the stitches she had begun to remove.

      @MINA
      I thought it needed fixing.

      @ELISE
      It does. By me, preferably.

      For the first time that day, Rafi smiles.
    notes: Use new information to complicate both positions, not declare a winner. Worked example. Adapt freely or use the companion outline to start your own story.
    extensions:
      x-skeleton:
        writing:
          version: 1
          format: fountain
          speakers:
            RAFI: char_1
            MINA: char_2
            ELISE: char_3
  - id: sc_3
    act_id: act_1
    header: INT. REPAIR SHOP - AFTERNOON
    loc:
      type: INT
      name: REPAIR SHOP
      tod: AFTERNOON
    shot_refs: []
    narrative: |-
      Mina threads a needle and sets it beside Elise, point away. She waits rather than taking the coat.

      Rafi checks his watch, then opens the folding chair he had packed away.

      @RAFI
      The community room is empty on Thursdays. I can ask.

      @MINA
      I'm not Mum.

      @RAFI
      No. You explain things slower.

      She gives him a look. He raises both hands.

      Elise completes one stitch. Mina turns the sleeve so she can see it.

      At four, the landlord finds the rails empty and three people at the counter. Rafi hands over the keys. Mina carries her sewing case. Elise wears the coat, with its small, imperfect rectangle intact.

      Outside, Mina holds the case out to Rafi.

      @MINA
      You can carry this.

      He does.

    act_id: act_1
    header: INT. LIBRARY - MORNING
    loc:
      type: INT
      name: LIBRARY
      tod: MORNING
    shot_refs: []
    narrative: |-
      The drawer labelled CLIMBING BEANS was empty. Yesterday it had held twelve paper packets, enough for every plot at planting day.

      Nia found a curl of blue thread caught on the handle. Under the drawer was a damp square on the floor. The empty display tray smelled faintly of rain.

      "Sam was last in," said Mr Okafor. "Blue jacket."

      Outside the window, Sam was unloading stakes beside the greenhouse. Nia almost went straight out. Then she remembered the librarian's own rule for cataloguing: write what you know before what you think.

      She wrote: thread, water, twelve missing packets. She did not write a name.

    act_id: act_1
    header: EXT. COMMUNITY GARDEN - MORNING
    loc:
      type: EXT
      name: COMMUNITY GARDEN
      tod: MORNING
    shot_refs: []
    narrative: |-
      Sam's jacket was blue nylon, smooth and bright. The thread on the drawer was soft, pale cotton.

      "I shut the greenhouse at six," Sam said. "Mr Okafor came back after the rain started. He was carrying a box."

      "Did you see what was in it?"

      "No. Ask him."

      On the greenhouse shelf, Nia saw twelve little mounds of soil, each beside a paper label. The labels bore the same hand-drawn climbing bean as the missing envelopes.

      She could have called that a solution. Instead she checked the library window. Above the seed drawer, the old frame was wet. A folded blue cleaning cloth lay on the sill, with one corner unravelled.
    notes: Let an apparent suspect supply useful evidence rather than exist only as a diversion. Worked example. Adapt freely or use the companion outline to start your own story.
    extensions:

          format: prose

    act_id: act_1
    header: INT. GREENHOUSE - DAY
    loc:
      type: INT
      name: GREENHOUSE
      tod: DAY
    shot_refs: []
    narrative: |-
      Mr Okafor listened while Nia set the thread beside the cloth.

      "The roof leaked last night," he said. "Some packets were soaked. I was afraid the seeds would rot. So I planted them."

      "All twelve?"

      "One pot per packet. Same labels. I meant to write a notice, but I thought I'd already ruined planting day."

      Nia looked at the careful rows. The beans hadn't been stolen. They had arrived at tomorrow early.

      Together they changed the notice to SEEDLINGS AVAILABLE SOON. Under it, Mr Okafor added his name and an explanation of the leak.

      When Sam came in, Nia handed over the stakes.

      "I nearly blamed your jacket," she said.

      Sam looked at the blue cloth. "That one is much more suspicious."

      They put a bucket under the window before they did anything else.

    narrative: |-
      ELENA sits beside a box of unsold buns. JUNE arrives with a tray of seedlings and tries to shelter them beneath her coat.

      Elena moves the box to her lap.

      @ELENA
      The tomatoes can have my seat.

      @JUNE
      They're peppers.

      @ELENA
      Then I owe them an apology.

      June sets the tray down. One small leaf sticks to Elena's sleeve. June points; Elena carefully lifts it free.

      tod: LATER
    shot_refs: []
    narrative: |-
      The timetable display changes to CANCELLED. Across the road, a different bus pulls in.

      @ELENA
      That's mine if I walk the long way.

      She stands, then hesitates.

      @JUNE
      I'm at the garden on Saturdays. Near the old cinema.

      @ELENA
      I work Saturdays.

      @JUNE
      Right.

      Elena looks at the buns. June looks at the rain. Neither moves.

      @ELENA
      I finish at two.

      June looks up.

      @JUNE
      I wasn't trying to sell you a pepper.

      @ELENA
      I was hoping you weren't.

    header: INT. ARCHIVE ROOM - MORNING

    shot_refs: []
    narrative: |-
      Every morning on the moon settlement, Sora watched eight minutes of an Earth sunrise. Her father had recorded it before the coastal station flooded: orange water, a gull, his sleeve accidentally crossing the lens.

      The archive screen marked it PRIVATE COPY. The public copy, cleaned of the sleeve and the sound of his breathing, took almost no space. Sora had never watched that one.

      Tavi arrived with the children's transmission. It contained a tour of the new greenhouse, three arguments about names for a beetle, and a song nobody finished in the same key.

      "The relay leaves in an hour," she said.

      The archive needed room for the local transmission buffer. Its display offered one file large enough to make that room.
    notes: Make the speculative rule concrete and connect it to a personal want. Worked example. Adapt freely or use the companion outline to start your own story.

    loc:
      type: INT

      tod: DAY
    shot_refs: []
    narrative: |-
      Sora asked Tavi to shorten the message.

      "We tried. Amil said you can't cut out the argument because then the beetle's name makes no sense."

      "Nobody on Earth needs six minutes about a beetle."

      Tavi looked through the greenhouse wall at the black sky. "We don't know what they need. We only know what happened here."

      Sora tried the spare archive cards. Two were dead. The third could hold the message or the sunrise, not both. The relay would not wait for a replacement shuttle.

      On the screen, her father's sleeve passed over the sun again. For years Sora had called it an error in the recording. Now she saw that the error was the part she had been keeping.

    header: INT. ARCHIVE ROOM - LATER
    loc:
      type: INT

      tod: LATER
    shot_refs: []
    narrative: |-
      Sora listened once more. Her father said, almost too quietly to hear, "There it is."

      She wrote the words on the inside cover of her notebook. Then she deleted the private copy and watched its name leave the screen.

      The children's transmission loaded. Sora checked the checksum, then let Tavi press SEND. A small blue light moved across the relay map.

      "Will they answer?" Tavi asked.

      "Not soon."

      "Will you miss it?"

      "Yes."

      They stayed until the light reached the edge of the map. On their way out, Tavi pulled her toward the greenhouse. The beetle was climbing a leaf. No one had recorded its first attempt or its second.

      They watched its third together. Sora opened her notebook, left a space beneath her father's words, and began to write.

  - id: sc_1
    act_id: act_1
    header: INT. SHADOW MENDER'S SHOP - EVENING
    loc:
      type: INT
      name: SHADOW MENDER'S SHOP
      tod: EVENING
    shot_refs: []
    narrative: |-
      Pip's own shadow was perfectly good at being Pip. This seemed a disappointing talent on the evening of the lantern parade.

      Aunt Ren unrolled a dragon shadow across her shop floor. Its paper-thin wings stretched under three chairs.

      "Until the last lantern goes out," she said. "Remember: a borrowed shadow follows your promises. Every one you make before it returns."

      Pip promised to bring it back undamaged. The dragon lifted its head.

      Outside, little Oli was waiting with an unlit rabbit lantern. He was frightened of the dark lane between his house and the square.

      "I'll walk with you," Pip said. "All the way."

      The dragon spread its wings, and Pip felt magnificent.
    notes: State a magical rule clearly enough for the ending to depend on it. Worked example. Adapt freely or use the companion outline to start your own story.

          version: 1
          format: prose
  - id: sc_2
    act_id: act_1
    header: EXT. LANTERN LANE - NIGHT
    loc:
      type: EXT
      name: LANTERN LANE
      tod: NIGHT
    shot_refs: []
    narrative: |-
      Halfway down the lane, Pip heard the parade drums. The dragon competition was starting. If they ran, they could still reach the front.

      "Just follow me," Pip told Oli, and hurried ahead.

      The dragon didn't move.

      Pip took another step. Their feet rose neatly off the ground. The shadow held them like a kite on a short string.

      Behind them, Oli's lantern shook.

      "I said I'd walk with you," Pip remembered.

      The dragon lowered Pip gently into a puddle. It was not an impressive entrance, even with wings.

      Pip went back. Together they lit Oli's lantern from a light in a neighbour's window. Then they walked slowly, because Oli's shoes were new and the stones were uneven.

    extensions:
      x-skeleton:

          version: 1
          format: prose
  - id: sc_3
    act_id: act_1
    header: EXT. PARADE SQUARE - NIGHT
    loc:
      type: EXT
      name: PARADE SQUARE
      tod: NIGHT
    shot_refs: []
    narrative: |-
      By the time they reached the square, the dragon prize had been awarded. Pip felt the disappointment all the way to their wet socks.

      But Oli was looking up. In the light of his rabbit lantern, the dragon shadow curved around both of them. Its wings made a little roof over the cobbles.

      "Will it eat my rabbit?" he asked.

      "Only if I promise it supper," Pip said.

      Oli laughed. They joined the back of the parade.

      At the shop, Pip returned the dragon before the final lantern dimmed. Aunt Ren checked its edges.

      "Undamaged," she said. "And you?"

      "A bit muddy."

      Pip's own shadow settled beneath their feet. It was still perfectly good at being Pip.

      When Oli asked for company on the walk home, that turned out to be exactly the right talent.
